tldr: Instead of directly predicting action values at discrete control steps, learning a vector field (Ordinary Differential Equation: ODE) that describes the rate of change of actions yields policies that are physically smooth and learn exceptionally fast.
hero_caption: Comparison between conventional methods and the proposed ODE policy. Conventional direct-action approaches output action values at discrete steps, often causing discontinuities at chunk boundaries (left). In contrast, ODE policy learns a vector field representing the rate of change of actions and integrates it over physical time, generating intrinsically smooth and continuous trajectories (right).
overview:
In current robot learning—both imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL)—direct-action policies that map observations directly to discrete action values dominate. However, because robots operate in a continuous physical world, real-world motions are inherently smooth. Conventional policies are forced to implicitly learn this smoothness and continuity from vast amounts of data, leading to abrupt trajectory jumps at chunk boundaries and requiring massive data and compute.

To solve this, the authors introduce the "ODE policy." Rather than modeling "actions themselves," it uses a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) to directly model the dynamics of the action—specifically, a velocity vector field describing how actions evolve over physical time. Conditioned on observations, the network outputs action derivatives, which are numerically integrated along physical time to generate trajectories. By integrating over short action chunks (or single RL steps) and seamlessly chaining from the previous action, control trajectories are guaranteed to be physically continuous by construction.

The authors evaluate ODE policy across simulations (the LIBERO benchmark and humanoid motion tracking) and four real-world robotic platforms (unimanual, bimanual, bimanual dexterous hands, and a full-sized humanoid) against 14 competitive baselines.

In imitation learning, ODE policy achieved overwhelming success rates after just a single epoch, surpassing large flow-matching and diffusion policies in data efficiency, parameter efficiency, and inference speed. It recorded the highest success rates across all 14 real-world tasks and moved even more smoothly than human demonstrations.
contributions: Proposed a new policy paradigm that directly models action dynamics (velocity vector fields) via Neural ODEs rather than predicting actions directly.
Developed a training framework with chunk-level numerical integration and contractive perturbations that enables ultra-fast, stable imitation learning.
Introduced a lightweight diversity head that supplies directional velocity offsets, preserving multi-modal action choices without iterative generation.

Demonstrated seamless integration not only in imitation learning but also in model-based RL (SuperMimic) and large foundation models (π0.5, ImageWAM, GR00T), consistently improving efficiency and motion smoothness.

sections.heading: Why Learn Motion Laws Instead of Action Values?
sections.summary: Existing robot policies regress or generate discrete action values, leaving the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. This paper proposes the "ODE policy," which learns an ordinary differential equation (ODE) governing continuous action changes and generates motions through numerical integration.
sections.details:
Robot learning via both IL and RL has progressed rapidly. Yet most methods follow the same direct-action paradigm: directly predicting future discrete action values from current observations. This direct mapping suffers from shared shortcomings. In IL, learning continuity demands enormous datasets and computation; when using generative models, multi-step inference per action chunk causes latency that impedes real-time control. In RL, control commands often oscillate between steps, exerting undue wear on robot joints.

Robots and humans alike are physical systems that move smoothly over time. Thus, rather than predicting action values, a policy should model the underlying law of motion—a vector field of how actions change—with a neural network and integrate it over physical time. This concept aligns well with neuroscience findings that animal motor cortex generates motor dynamics.

The proposed ODE policy employs a Neural ODE to learn an observation-conditioned velocity field of actions. In IL, actions are integrated over chunks and supervised against demonstration trajectories; in RL, integration proceeds step by step. At deployment, each chunk is integrated starting from the previous chunk's terminal action, structurally eliminating jerks across boundaries. Furthermore, a lightweight diversity head allows the policy to capture multi-modal behaviors when multiple paths exist.

captions.F2: Comparison between direct-action policies (left) and ODE policy (right). Conventional methods independently predict discrete actions, often causing discontinuities at chunk boundaries. ODE policy integrates the same vector field over physical time, smoothly continuing from the end of the previous chunk.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Prior Dynamical Systems and Diffusion Models?
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes its approach across three lines of prior work: dynamical systems for motion generation, state-space dynamics models, and generative diffusion/flow models. It highlights the novelty of directly learning unconstrained vector fields of actions along the physical time axis.
sections.details:
The positioning of this work becomes clear when compared against three established research directions.

### ODE as Action Dynamics
Using differential equations for robot motion generation has a rich history, such as Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) and stable dynamical systems. However, these methods typically constrain the functional form of vector fields or enforce convergence to predefined attractors, limiting them to narrow sets of motions. ODE policy places no artificial constraints on the vector field, learning diverse tasks end-to-end within a single general neural network.

### ODE as State Dynamics
Modeling robot or environment state transitions using Neural ODEs to build controllers is also common. However, these frameworks integrate states or latent representations, leaving action values to be decoded separately. ODE policy fundamentally differs by integrating the time derivative of actions themselves.

### ODE as Generative Process
Diffusion policies and flow matching also solve differential equations internally, but their integration occurs along a virtual denoising time axis completely detached from physical time. Intermediate states have no physical meaning. In contrast, ODE policy integrates along real-world physical time, smoothly generating future actions from the terminal state of past actions.

sections.heading: Direct-Action Policies and Neural ODE Fundamentals
sections.summary: This section outlines standard formulations of direct-action policies in IL (regression, diffusion, flow matching) and RL, and reviews the core mechanics of Neural ODEs and their gradient computation techniques.
sections.details:
### Direct-Action Policies
Given conditions $\mathbf{c}_t$ derived from visual observations $\mathbf{o}_t$ or language instructions $\mathbf{l}_t$, alongside proprioceptive states $\mathbf{s}_t$, conventional policies directly predict action values $\mathbf{a}_t$. In IL, action chunking—predicting a sequence of $H$ future steps—is standard. However, because each step is generated independently, continuity across steps and chunks must be learned implicitly from data. Simple regression tends to average multi-modal distributions, while diffusion models and flow matching achieve high sample quality at the cost of iterative inference across virtual time steps.

### Neural ODEs
A Neural ODE parameterizes the time derivative of a continuous state $\mathbf{x}(t)$ with a neural network $\mathbf{g}_\phi(\mathbf{x}(t), t)$. Trajectories are computed by integrating from an initial state using numerical solvers (such as Euler or RK4). Gradients of the loss with respect to network parameters are computed either by backpropagating directly through the solver's computational graph or via the adjoint state method for memory efficiency. This paper repurposes this formulation for robotic action trajectory generation.

sections.heading: How ODE Policy Works: Vector Fields, Contractive Perturbations, and Diversity Head
sections.summary: The network models the velocity of action changes and integrates over short chunks to fit demonstrations. Key innovations include contractive perturbations to prevent drift on real hardware, a diversity head for multi-modal actions, and an adaptation for reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
### Vector Field Formulation and Chunk Integration
Conditioned on visual/language embeddings $\mathbf{z}_t$ and proprioceptive states $\mathbf{s}_t$, the network models action velocity: $\dot{\mathbf{a}}(t) = \mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{a}(t), \mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{z}_t)$. At decision step $t$, the policy takes the terminal action of the previous chunk $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{t-1}$ as the initial state and integrates numerically over physical time for $H$ steps to produce the action chunk. Because the network takes current action $\mathbf{a}(t)$ as input, it produces self-consistent trajectories where the current action position dictates its rate of change.

### Training Loss and Contractive Perturbations
During training, the policy integrates for $H$ steps starting from the demonstration action and minimizes the path loss against the ground-truth trajectory. Because chunks are short, gradients can be backpropagated directly through solver steps without the adjoint method. However, training strictly on demonstration trajectories leaves the policy vulnerable to compounding drift at deployment. To resolve this, the authors introduce contractive perturbations: adding a random offset $\bm{\delta}$ to the initial action and supervising the integration to contract geometrically back toward the demonstration trajectory. This creates an attractor basin around the nominal path, dramatically enhancing robustness to disturbances.

### Seamless Chunking at Inference
During inference, rather than starting integration from measured robot states, the policy begins from the commanded target action $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{t-1}$ of the previous chunk. This produces completely continuous trajectories without boundary jumps. Furthermore, actions can be streamed to low-level controllers as each integration step completes, without waiting for the full chunk to finish.

### Diversity Head for Multi-Modal Behaviors
A purely deterministic vector field suffers from mode averaging—such as colliding with a central obstacle when left and right bypasses are both valid. To address this, a lightweight diversity head samples an offset velocity from a Gaussian mixture model at chunk initiation. Slightly perturbing the field direction steers the entire integrated trajectory into distinct modes, preserving multi-modal behaviors without multi-step generative loops.

### Reinforcement Learning Formulation
In RL, where no demonstrations exist, chunk length is set to $H=1$, integrating single Euler steps from the previous action. This architecture allows policy gradients to flow backwards across action sequences without vanishing, accelerating training significantly.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup: From Simulation to Four Real-World Robots
sections.summary: The authors designed an extensive experimental suite spanning LIBERO simulation, large pretrained models (VLAs and WAMs), model-based RL (SuperMimic), and four physical robot setups (single-arm, dual-arm, hand, humanoid), evaluated against 14 baselines.
sections.details:
To evaluate ODE policy across four core axes—learning speed, inference speed and smoothness, generalization, and multi-modality—the authors conducted comprehensive experiments.

### Benchmark Environments
- **Visuomotor IL**: Evaluated on all 4 suites (40 tasks) of LIBERO, with zero-shot generalization tested on perturbed LIBERO-plus.
- **Action Head for Foundation Models**: Evaluated as the action head for $\pi_{0.5}$ (a 2.9B parameter VLA) and ImageWAM (a 3.9B image-world-action model).
- **Reinforcement Learning**: Evaluated as the actor in SuperMimic for whole-body humanoid motion tracking on a Unitree G1.
- **Real-World Robotics**: Tested on 14 tasks across four hardware setups: Franka single arm, Galaxea R1 Lite dual-arm, Sharpa dexterous hand, and a Unitree G1 full-sized humanoid equipped with Inspire hands. This included zero-shot transfer using public datasets (SharpaDex) collected in external labs.

### Baselines
Comparisons were made against 14 competitive baselines, including flow matching (FM-DiT, FM-UNet), diffusion models (DDPM-DiT, DDPM-UNet, DDIM-UNet), A2A-DiT, and ACT. For rigorous comparison, visual encoders, datasets, and training schedules were kept identical across methods.

sections.heading: Simulation Results: Exceptional Learning Efficiency and Trajectory Smoothness
sections.summary: On LIBERO, ODE policy achieved a 79.2% success rate in just 1 epoch, matching flow-matching performance with under half the data. Inference was over 10x faster, and action jerk was the lowest among all baselines.
sections.details:
### Learning Efficiency (Data and Parameter Efficiency)
In LIBERO imitation learning, ODE policy demonstrated rapid learning from the very first epoch. After 1 epoch, it reached a 79.2% success rate, nearly doubling the strongest baseline (~43%). It achieved 85% success in just 2 epochs, orders of magnitude faster than flow matching (30 epochs) and diffusion models (50–60 epochs).
In data efficiency, ODE policy trained on only 20 demonstrations per task (87.7%) outperformed FM-DiT trained on all 50 demonstrations (85.4%). Furthermore, scaling parameters down to 1.5M still surpassed a 48M FM-DiT.

### Foundation Models and Reinforcement Learning
Replacing the 430M action expert of $\pi_{0.5}$ with a 13.7M ODE head (~3% of parameters) achieved a 96.0% success rate after 1 epoch from random initialization (vs. 75.5% for randomly initialized FM). Similarly, on ImageWAM, it outperformed FM in the first epoch (82.6% vs. 24.6%). In RL with SuperMimic, unhindered gradient propagation backward in time led to consistently higher early returns.

### Inference Cost and Motion Smoothness
Using an Euler solver, generating an 8-action chunk took only 5.7 ms—10.8x faster than FM-DiT and ~100x faster than DDPM. End-effector jerk was lower than all baselines across checkpoints, and average completion steps were the shortest.

### Multi-Modal Navigation
In a 2D multi-path navigation task requiring traversal through one of four narrow gaps, ODE policy with a diversity head balanced all four modes starting from epoch 1, maintaining high mode balance metrics.

sections.heading: Real-World Evaluations: Outperforming Baselines Across All 14 Tasks
sections.summary: Evaluations across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous hand, and humanoid platforms revealed superior performance in precision insertion, cloth folding, zero-shot transfer, and whole-body loco-manipulation across all 14 real-world tasks.
sections.details:
### Unimanual Robot (Franka Research 3)
Four tasks were evaluated: packing a mango and closing a box, hanging a key on a hook, folding a sock into a drawer, and block insertion. In contact-rich tasks like sock folding (15/20 successes) and block insertion (14/20 successes), ODE policy outperformed baselines (which maxed out at 8/20 and 4/20). Joint angular acceleration at chunk boundaries was markedly lower.

### Bimanual Robot (Galaxea R1 Lite)
Tasks included inserting a thin flower stem into a vase, placing a bowl into a microwave and closing the door, sequential double-flower insertion, and a multi-modal drawer task. In the drawer task, demonstrations evenly balanced two modes: left hand inserts apple / right hand closes drawer, and vice versa. With its diversity head, ODE policy successfully executed both strategies on physical hardware with a 60% success rate.

### Dexterous Hand (Sharpa)
Beyond can pick-and-place, the authors evaluated zero-shot transfer using SharpaDex, an open dataset collected in a different lab environment, with no fine-tuning. ODE policy succeeded in cup uprighting (17/20 vs. 0/20 for FM-DiT) and pill transfer between cups (17/20 vs. 10/20 for FM-DiT), demonstrating strong environmental adaptability.

### Humanoid (Unitree G1)
Tasks required walking to pick up a toy from the floor, crouching, and stowing it in a sofa box, as well as picking a rice ball from a table, turning around, and placing it inside a microwave. Replacing the action head of GR00T N1.7 stabilized walking, balance, and manipulation coordination, doubling overall task success rates from 30–35% to 60–70%.

captions.F11: Four tasks on the Franka single-arm robot: box packing, key hanging, sock folding, and block insertion. In all tasks, ODE policy achieved the highest success rates after only 50 epochs of training compared to DDPM, DDIM, FM, and A2A baselines.
captions.F12: Four tasks on the Galaxea bimanual robot: (A) narrow vase insertion, (B) microwave bowl placement, (C) sequential two-flower insertion, and (D) multi-modal drawer task clearing an apple with either arm. ODE policy achieved smoother, higher-precision control throughout.
captions.F14: Whole-body loco-manipulation (locomotion, crouching, manipulation) on the Unitree G1 humanoid: (A) picking and boxing a floor toy, and (B) microwave rice ball placement. Success rates doubled compared to GR00T's native head.

sections.heading: Ablation Studies: What Drives the Performance Gains?
sections.summary: Systematic ablations on chunk length, ODE numerical solvers, contractive perturbations, seamless chunking, and proprioception injection points reveal the core factors behind ODE policy's success.
sections.details:
Ablation experiments systematically isolated the impact of each design component:

- **Chunk Length $H$**: At $H=1$ (per-step image processing), success dropped to 76.4%. In modern IL, action chunking is vital to suppress compounding error; $H=8$ struck the optimal balance between accuracy and computational cost.
- **Numerical Solver Choice**: Replacing higher-order Runge-Kutta solvers (RK4, RK2) with a simple Euler method caused less than a 1% change in final success. This confirms that high-precision integration is not the critical factor; rather, the ODE formulation of integrating a single vector field across physical time is what matters. Using Euler maximizes training and inference speed.
- **Contractive Perturbations**: Removing contractive perturbations caused epoch 1 success to plummet from 79.8% to 58.4%. Perturbations prevent early, imperfect vector fields from diverging away from demonstration manifolds.
- **Seamless Chunking**: Integrating from measured robot joint states instead of previous chunk terminal targets re-introduced boundary jumps, increasing jerk by 1.3–2.2x and reducing epoch 1 success to 47.8%.
- **Proprioception Routing**: Injecting proprioceptive state directly into the velocity field network yielded far more stable early training than concatenating it with visual tokens before processing.

sections.heading: Discussion and Future Directions: Action-Free Data, Arbitrary Frequencies, and Motor Intent
sections.summary: The authors discuss broader implications of the ODE framework: enabling velocity feedforward on action-free teleoperation data, variable control frequencies at deployment, handling discrete actions, and neuroscience parallels in unfolding motor intent.
sections.details:
Framing robot policies as continuous-time vector fields opens capabilities unavailable to direct-action paradigms.

### Learning from Action-Free Datasets
Handheld capturing devices like UMI or human video demonstrations log observed poses without target control commands, causing lag in trained policies. ODE policy extracts target velocities at zero extra cost, which can be fed directly into PD controller damping terms as feedforward velocity. In long-horizon tasks, this boosted completion rates from 51% to 72%.

### Arbitrary Control Frequencies
Because the vector field is continuous in time, changing the solver's integration step size allows zero-shot execution at higher frequencies—such as scaling a policy trained at 20 Hz to 40 Hz or 80 Hz at deployment without retraining. Physical robot tests confirmed robust execution at varying rates.

### Discrete Action Signals (Grippers)
Because ODEs assume continuous transitions, predicting binary gripper commands via a separate classification head was most stable. Embedding binary signals into ODE dimensions slightly reduced performance, though it still outperformed baselines. Incorporating hybrid dynamical systems or jump processes represents an exciting future direction.

### Unfolding Motor Intent (Neuroscience Analogy)
Motor cortex in primates is thought not to encode end-point kinematics statically, but rather to unfold continuous motion dynamics from a prepared state. ODE policy mirrors this mechanism: discrete behavioral intent is selected at chunk initiation, and continuous physical motion unfolds smoothly along the vector field.

takeaways: Learning action velocities (vector fields) rather than raw action values guarantees physical smoothness by construction, yielding massive gains in learning speed and data efficiency.
Using a lightweight Euler solver matches the accuracy of complex RK4 integrators, drastically slashing compute costs for real-time control.
Combining seamless chunking (chaining from previous targets) with contractive perturbations (pulling off-manifold states back) is key to stable trajectory tracking on real robots.
A learned vector field supports arbitrary control frequencies at inference by simply adjusting the integration step size, accommodating varying robot hardware without retraining.
limitations: Inherently continuous ODE formulations struggle with discrete signals like binary gripper states, requiring dedicated classification heads for best performance.
In model-free RL settings where discrete exploration jumps are necessary, ODE-enforced trajectory smoothing can hinder exploration.
Sharp impacts or rigid collisions can violate continuous velocity assumptions; incorporating contact event detection or hybrid dynamical systems remains future work.
